meaning: Training on unlabeled data with a made-up task whose answer is already in the data (match two views, fill in a hidden part), then reusing the learned features with few labels.
The self-made task used in SSL (predict a rotation, solve a jigsaw, find the twin view, repaint masked patches). You keep the features, not the task.
Pull two augmentations of the same input together and push other inputs apart. InfoNCE is a softmax cross-entropy over similarities divided by a temperature, where the right answer is the twin.
Every input maps to (nearly) the same embedding: positives look perfectly similar, but the features are useless. Prevented by negatives, a momentum teacher, or centering and sharpening.
tools: monitor embedding spread or kNN accuracy

meaning: A copy of the network whose weights are a slow moving average of the student's and receive no gradient; the student learns to match its outputs, which avoids collapse without negatives.
Hide a large share of image patches (75%) and train a ViT to reconstruct them; the encoder only processes the visible patches, so pretraining is cheap.
A single linear layer trained on frozen features (or a hidden layer) to test whether some information is linearly decodable there. Decodable does not mean the model uses it.
A network for graph-shaped data (molecules, roads, social networks) that updates each node from its neighbours with shared weights, so it works for any graph size and node order.
One GNN round: each node aggregates its neighbours' vectors with an order-free function (sum, mean, max) and updates its own vector. k rounds let a node see k hops away.
Invariance: renumbering the nodes doesn't change a whole-graph output. Equivariance: renumbering the nodes renumbers the per-node outputs the same way.
Graph Convolutional Network (Kipf and Welling): add self-loops, average neighbours with weights 1/√(deg·deg), then apply a shared linear layer: H′ = D^−½ (A + I) D^−½ H W.
A GNN that samples a fixed number of neighbours per hop (for example 25 then 10) and learns an aggregation function, so it scales to huge graphs and handles nodes unseen in training.
Graph Attention Network: learns a score per edge and softmaxes over a node's neighbours, so important neighbours count more. A transformer is attention on a complete graph.
With many GNN layers, repeated neighbour averaging makes all node vectors nearly identical, so nodes can no longer be told apart. Why most GNNs use 2–4 layers.
A sequence layer built on a linear recurrence (state = A·state + B·input), computable as a loop for generation or as a convolution or parallel scan for training, with a fixed-size state.
An SSM whose step size Δ and matrices B, C depend on the current token, so it chooses what to write into its state and what to ignore. Mamba-2 runs as matrix multiplies (SSD).
The stored keys and values of all past tokens that a transformer keeps for generation; it grows with context: 2 × KV heads × head dim × bytes × layers per token.
An LLM that uses mostly SSM layers plus a few attention layers (Jamba 1 : 7, Granite 4.0 9 : 1), keeping most of the memory savings and most of attention's exact recall.
A heat map of the gradient of the output with respect to each input: which inputs would change the answer most. Cheap, but local, noisy and blind where the model is saturated.
Attribution that averages input gradients along a straight path from a baseline to the input and multiplies by the input change; the attributions add up to output(input) − output(baseline).
Randomize the model's weights (or train on random labels) and compare explanations; a method whose maps barely change isn't explaining the model (Adebayo et al., 2018).
A network storing more features than it has neurons, as non-orthogonal directions, when features are sparse; individual neurons then respond to several unrelated things.
An overcomplete autoencoder with an L1 penalty, trained on a model's activations so each latent tends to capture one interpretable (monosemantic) feature.
A pair of attention heads that completes the pattern [A][B] … [A] → [B]: find the previous occurrence of the current token and predict what followed it. A key mechanism of in-context copying.
An input changed by a small, deliberately chosen perturbation so a model gets it wrong. In high dimensions, aligned changes of ε per input add up to ε·m·n in the score.
Fast gradient sign method: x_adv = x + ε·sign(∇ₓ loss). One backward pass; underestimates vulnerability compared with iterative attacks.
Projected gradient descent: repeat small sign steps and project back into the ε-box around the input. The standard attack for evaluating robustness and for adversarial training.
Training on attacked (usually PGD) versions of each batch, minimizing the worst-case loss in the ε-box. The most reliable empirical defense; costs training time and some clean accuracy.
A model is calibrated when “p% confident” is right p% of the time. Expected calibration error averages |accuracy − confidence| over confidence bins, weighted by bin size.
Divide all logits by one number T fitted on validation NLL; fixes most overconfidence (T > 1) without changing any prediction's class.
Aleatoric: noise in the data itself, which more data can't remove. Epistemic: the model's ignorance where it has little data; it shrinks with data and shows up as disagreement between models.
Uncertainty from several predictions: an ensemble of independently trained networks (M = 5 is typical), or one network run many times with dropout left on. Disagreement signals epistemic uncertainty.
Flagging inputs unlike the training data with a score (max softmax, energy, ensemble disagreement) and a threshold set on normal data, then routing them to a fallback.
The deployed data differs from training: covariate shift changes the inputs p(x), label shift changes the class mix p(y), concept shift changes the rule p(y | x).
